abstract: Telomeres are maintained by telomerase, where the reverse transcriptase TERT copies a template in the telomerase RNA (TR). How TERT evolves when its RNA partner duplicates and diverges is unknown. In monkeyflowers (Mimulus), a TR duplication arose in the ancestor of the Erythranthe group but the derived paralog (TR2) remains functional only in M. lewisii, whose telomeres consist of two repeat types. Using new genome assemblies, we found that TERT evolved rapidly in the Erythranthe group with the strongest signal in the N-terminal TR-binding domain (TRBD). Most amino acid changes occurred on the ancestral branch carrying the TR duplication. In yeast three-hybrid assays, M. lewisii TERT bound both the ancestral (TR1) and derived (TR2) paralogs, whereas TERT from species without a functional TR2 did not bind TR2. Binding of both paralogs required two M. lewisii-specific residues near the KRxR motif of the TRBD. We developed TRAPNGS (Telomeric Repeat Amplification Protocol followed by next-generation sequencing) and discovered M. lewisii telomerase was more active than that of related species without an increase in TERT expression. In hybrids between M. lewisii and M. verbenaceus, telomeres on M. verbenaceus chromosomes acquired M. lewisii-type repeats and length within one generation. These results suggest that TR duplication can shape the evolution of TERT, enhance the telomerase activity, and alter the telomere composition.
